newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: China set for diplomatic triumph at UN rights body.
newsitem.headline: China set for diplomatic triumph at UN rights body.

text.p: China was on track for a diplomatic triumph on Tuesday at the U.N. Human Rights Commission where a Western-backed resolution criticising Beijing's rights record appeared doomed, diplomats said.
China's delegation to the 53-member forum seemed to have won enough support among Asian and non-aligned states to block even holding a vote on the motion tabled by Denmark, they said.
This would make it the seventh year in a row, starting the year after the June 1989 Chinese crackdown in Tiananmen Square, that China has emerged without censure by the main U.N.human rights body.
"It looks like a diplomatic triumph for China," said one diplomat at the annual six-week session which ends on Friday.
"Everything is going China's way. The numbers are not there for anything else," another said.

Amid continuing reports of repression in China, concern over the world's most populous country has been greater than ever at the U.N. session in Geneva this year, due to the prospect of Hong Kong reverting to the mainland on June 30.
The showdown -- expected after 1700 GMT -- follows a fierce lobbying campaign by China on one side and pressure by the United States and some European states on the other.
A U.S. government official in Geneva last week accused Beijing of using "economic and political" threats to get votes.

As in previous years, Wu Jianmin, China's ambassador to the U.N. in Geneva and head of delegation, is expected to pre-empt any vote on the Danish resolution by presenting Beijing's own "no-action motion", according to U.N. sources.

Last year, 27 states voted in favour of the Chinese motion, 20 voted against and six abstaine, quashing any vote on the European Union text. Only in 1995 did China lose its no-action motion but went on to defeat the Western resolution.
U.S Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has called on foreign ministers of Commission members to rally support for the Danish resolution, the State Department said on Monday.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, speaking to reporters in Washington, did not say if Albright felt she had succeeded in winning support from Germany and Spain, both NATO allies, or Australia, also a close friend of the United States.

Denmark was obliged to step into the breach as sponsor of the motion on China after France and Germany backed away from supporting the traditional European Union resolution. The voting intentions of Greece and Italy remained unclear, diplomats said.

Burns said the United States believed "that as the world's premier multilateral human rights forum, the Human Rights Commission is a particularly appropriate venue" for discussing China's rights record.

"And we hope very much that the other countries ...will take a stand in favour of the universality of human rights principles and that they will vote with Denmark and the United States and other countries to bring the issue to the floor for a formal discussion and for a vote," he added.

In Geneva, Assistant Secretary of State John Shattuck told a news conference on Monday: "We do not seek confrontation with China but we do seek greater respect for the rule of law and for acceptance of basic principles set forth in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights."

Shattuck said the United States recognised that China has undergone "significant transformation" through economic reforms that had brought greater well-being for ordinary people "and greater scope for individual choice."

"Nevertheless, China's government continues to commit widespread and well-documented human rights violations and to severely restrict fundamental freedoms of speech, the press, assembly, association and religion, in violation of internationally-established norms," he declared.
